survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary data from the German TALIS video study (national substudy of the international TALIS video study). The analytic sample is constructed from video-recorded mathematics lessons on quadratic equations, with additional inclusion/exclusion based on video quality and the availability of rated segments (human-coded and model-only segments). The paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or any specific TALIS weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights) in the statistical analyses; instead, it applies multilevel manifest modeling in Mplus with maximum likelihood estimation and robust standard errors. Because the outcomes are derived from video-based computer vision scoring and post-lesson questionnaires/observer ratings, the manuscript provides no explicit weighting strategy for population-representative inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use plausible values (PV) because the key dependent variables are video-based nonverbal immediacy scores produced by a computer-vision model and questionnaire/observer ratings on Likert-type scales, not cognitive achievement PVs. Missingness is handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) for the third video/lesson where four teachers lacked data; FIML is treated here as multiple imputation per the provided mapping. The paper reports that there were no missing data for posttest survey measures and for lesson-specific data for videos 1 and 2, so missingness is limited to a specific subset of the longitudinal video component.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the German TALIS video study implemented as a national substudy of the international TALIS video study (2016–2020). It includes 50 teachers and their 1,140 students from Grades 8–10 across 38 schools, but for the ML-based NVI algorithm development it excludes 4 teachers due to unavailable or low-quality video material, leaving 46 teachers. For the main analyses, it uses videos 1–3 to examine NVI variability (RQ1), but excludes video 3 for RQ2 because teacher- and student-reported support dimensions were assessed after the posttest and referred only to the first two recorded lessons. Within videos, only segments suitable for computer vision analysis are retained (no excessive camera movement, teacher fully visible, teacher remains in frame), and segments are selected using stratified sampling across teacher and lesson time; 403 segments were human-rated for model development, partitioned into teacher-disjoint training (324) and validation (79), and then an additional 220 segments were automatically annotated by the validated model. For the third video/lesson, four teachers lacked data and this missingness is handled with FIML.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (2016–2020) — German national substudy; Mathematics quadratic equations; Grades 8–10; video segments (30-s) within lessons
main_findings.performance_metrics: Variance components/ICC1: Teacher level ICCteacher=0.225 (22.5% variance), Lesson level ICClesson=0.056 (5.6%), Situation level ICCsituation=0.717 (71.7%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (German national substudy) data with mathematics quadratic-equations lessons and 30-s video segments, the study leveraged teacher-level covariates (teacher gender, teaching experience, and school type) to analyze how nonverbal immediacy (NVI) varies across teachers, lessons, and teaching situations, finding that 22.5% of NVI variance was between teachers while 71.7% was at the situation level. This indicates that NVI is not a purely stable teacher trait and that teacher training and feedback should target situationally responsive nonverbal behaviors rather than only person-level characteristics.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (2016–2020) — German national substudy; Mathematics quadratic equations; post-lesson surveys; observer ratings (16-min) matched to NVI (30-s)
main_findings.target_variable: Socioemotional support (encouragement and warmth) predicted by ML-assessed NVI
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level path model (Model 1) fit: χ2=0.062, df=1, CFI=1.00, RMSEA=0.000, SRMRwithin=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel2=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel3=0.007. Significant positive effects of NVI (ML) on socioemotional support (O): Level 1 β=0.14, SE=0.06, p=0.019; Level 2 β=0.35, SE=0.08, p=0.000; Level 3 β=0.43, SE=0.10, p=0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (German national substudy) data with matched ML-assessed NVI and observer-rated socioemotional support, the study leveraged observer socioemotional support and autonomy-support dimensions to model socioemotional support as an outcome, finding that ML-assessed NVI was positively and significantly related to observer-rated encouragement and warmth at the situation, lesson, and teacher levels. This indicates that strengthening teachers’ nonverbal immediacy behaviors may support a warmer, more encouraging classroom climate, though the design is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (2016–2020) — German national substudy; Mathematics quadratic equations; post-lesson surveys
main_findings.target_variable: Autonomy support predicted by ML-assessed NVI
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 1 (autonomy support) fit: χ2=0.062, df=1, CFI=1.00, RMSEA=0.000, SRMRwithin=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel2=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel3=0.007. Significant positive effects of NVI (ML) on autonomy support: Level 3 (teacher level) teacher-rated autonomy support β=0.36, SE=0.10, p=0.001; student-rated autonomy support β=0.25, SE=0.12, p=0.043. Non-significant teacher gender/work-experience effects on autonomy support at teacher level (teacher gender p=0.622; teaching experience p=0.817).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (German national substudy) data from post-lesson autonomy-support questionnaires matched to ML-assessed NVI, the study leveraged teacher and student autonomy-support measures alongside NVI to predict autonomy support, finding that ML-assessed NVI was significantly and positively related to both teacher-reported and student-reported autonomy support at the teacher level. This indicates that teacher development efforts that improve nonverbal immediacy may also align with need-supportive (autonomy-supportive) teaching practices, though causality cannot be inferred from the observational multilevel associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (2016–2020) — German national substudy; Mathematics quadratic equations; post-lesson surveys
main_findings.target_variable: Positive student–teacher relationships predicted by ML-assessed NVI
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 2 (relationships) fit: χ2=0.127, df=1, CFI=1.00, RMSEA=0.000, SRMRwithin=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel2=0.000, SRMRbetweenLevel3=0.012. NVI (ML) effects on positive relationships were not significant: teacher-rated relationships (T) at Level 3 β=-0.17, SE=0.14, p=0.239; student-rated relationships (S) at Level 3 β=0.12, SE=0.14, p=0.371. Teacher-rated and student-rated relationships were significantly correlated (w=0.57, SE=0.11, p=0.000).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (German national substudy) data from post-lesson relationship questionnaires matched to ML-assessed NVI, the study leveraged NVI and teacher covariates to predict positive student–teacher relationships, finding that ML-assessed NVI was not significantly related to either teacher-reported or student-reported positive relationships. This indicates that nonverbal immediacy may be more closely tied to autonomy-supportive and socioemotional climate aspects than to broader relationship quality, suggesting that teacher training should combine nonverbal immediacy with additional relational practices (e.g., fairness, belonging) to improve perceived relationships.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the German TALIS video study (2016–2020 international design; national substudy) with mathematics lessons on quadratic equations taught by 50 teachers and their 1,140 students (Grades 8–10). It develops a computer-vision-based ML algorithm to score teachers’ nonverbal immediacy (NVI) from classroom video, using human ratings of 403 segments (3,056 frames) for training/validation and then applying the validated model to additional segments, yielding 623 segments for analysis. In multilevel three-level manifest modeling, the best-supported pattern is that ML-assessed NVI is positively associated with observer-rated socioemotional support (encouragement and warmth) and with both teacher- and student-reported autonomy support, with significant standardized effects at multiple levels (e.g., Level 3 NVI→socioemotional support β=0.43, p=0.001; NVI→teacher autonomy support β=0.36, p=0.001). By contrast, NVI is not significantly related to positive student–teacher relationships. The analysis is correlational (no causal identification) and the manuscript does not report the use of TALIS complex survey weights; missingness for the third lesson is handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML).
